text: Lesson 24 settled the design on paper. Now build it for real: a table created from scratch in Studio, its form and list configured, and the one record type that actually makes it reachable by anyone other than you.

Both tables start the same way: Create Application File, Table, then two fields that matter most. Label is the human-readable name. Name is the real database table name, automatically prefixed with your scope. Extends is the field that implements Lesson 24's decision directly — set to task for Room Booking, inheriting state, assignment group, and priority immediately, and left blank for Room, producing a clean standalone table with none of that baggage.

Next, the reference field Lesson 24 planned. On Room Booking, create a field named room, set its Type to Reference, and its Reference to the Room table. That's the exact mechanism that displays a readable room name on screen while storing a sys_id underneath — planned on paper last lesson, built for real here.

Two more steps make the table genuinely usable, both straight out of Course 2's Forms and Lists chapter. Form Layout moves fields onto the actual form and groups them into sections — a request section, an approval section. List Layout chooses which columns show when someone views Room Booking as a list, so an approver scanning the list sees short_description, room, and state without opening every record.

Here's the part that surprises new developers. Room Booking is now completely built — dictionary, form, list — and it still has zero entries in the Application Navigator. The navigator only displays modules, not tables directly. The fix is a real record: Create Application File, Module, Link type set to List of Records, pointed at Room Booking. The table itself doesn't change at all, but it goes from invisible to one click away the instant that module is saved.

A table, its form, its list, and the module that finally makes it reachable — four distinct steps, each one real. Lesson 26 goes deeper on that last piece: the Application Menu and the different kinds of modules a custom app can use.
